Environmental Sciences: Where Earth’s Systems meet Human Solutions

The international BSc Environmental Sciences programme (BES) is a truly interdisciplinary programme which teaches students high-quality environmental sciences and equips them with important skills to address contemporary global environmental and sustainability challenges as responsible change makers. Based at one of the leading life sciences universities in the world, the BES programme takes a unique position in environmental sciences education in the Netherlands and internationally.

The programme includes core challenges associated with planetary boundaries, such as climate change, the depletion of natural resources, environmental pollution, the loss of biodiversity and water scarcity. Environmental Sciences focuses on the observation and analysis of these problems, as well as on the design, development and exploration of innovative and sustainable solutions. The programme teaches students to address complex and often transboundary environmental issues haracterized by uncertainties, lack of knowledge, diverging social interests, and conflicting views. As environmental and sustainability issues have societal causes and consequences that are linked through physical, chemical, and biological processes, students learn the required knowledge and understanding of the principles, methods, terminology and integration and application of both natural and social sciences. The programme also equips students with core academic, professional and personal skills to contribute to the transformation towards a more sustainable society, such as research design, systems thinking, data skills and GIS, collaboration, and integrating diverse types of knowledge and perspectives.

In the common part of the programme, students get a mix of courses that provide a solid foundation in natural and social sciences, while immediately mobilising this knowledge in skills-heavy integration courses with real-life problem-based national and international cases. Students learn how to do research and how to reflect on environmental challenges and theories, culminating in an individual BSc thesis project. Personal leadership skills are fostered from the start, helping students to develop their own path in the programme and become a responsible change maker for science and society.

The programme offers a choice between four specialisations:

  • Environmental Policy, Economics, and Law, focusing on the societal causes of environmental and sustainability issues, and on socio-political arrangements, and legal and economic instruments for prevention and control;
  • Environmental Quality and Ecosystems, focusing - within a systems approach framework - on the processes in and between the environmental compartments soil, water, and air that determine the fate of contaminants and their effects on organisms and ecosystems;
  • Environmental Technology for Circularity, focusing on the application of biological, physical, and chemical processes in techniques aimed at improving environmental quality, preventing or controlling emissions, and recovering valuable resources for reuse;
  • Interdisciplinary Environmental Challenges, focusing on using a systems perspective to integrate disciplinary and interdisciplinary knowledge to analyse complex environmental challenges and develop integrated solutions.

Free space in the third year allows the students to create a distinct profile for themselves, enhance their international experience, get hands-on professional experience, or become acquainted with other fields of study.

Bachelor’s in Environmental Sciences

Bachelor's in Environmental Sciences

Facts & figures
  • Climate, Society, Nature
  • Full-time
  • 3 Years
  • English
  • Wageningen
Apply now

Is this bachelor’s right for me?

About

Do you want to make a positive impact on the environment? By helping to tackle climate change and supporting sustainability? Then you’ll feel right at home in the BSc Environmental Sciences.

 

Curious? Come experience it for yourself during a Taster Day.

Taster Day

What makes this programme unique?

Mix of disciplines

The mix of natural, social and technological sciences gives you a complete picture of the relationship between people and the environment.

International network

Because this programme attracts many international students, you’ll learn to work together in diverse, international teams.

Worldwide Impact

Working towards a sustainable future is more urgent than ever! WUR's international network can help you make a global impact.


 

Source of precious knowledge

You’ll study environmental issues on a campus where we’ve been building and applying knowledge for over 100 years. A world of opportunities is waiting for you!

What you will learn

Your focus

In the Bachelor’s programme in Environmental Sciences, you'll learn how to look at major environmental and sustainability problems from different perspectives. You'll gain the knowledge and skills to devise smart solutions that consider both nature and society.

You will learn

  • You'll research environmental challenges such as pollution, resource shortages, and the transition to sustainable energy.
  • You'll learn to view nature, technology, and society from a perspective to develop sustainable solutions.
  • You'll use scientific research and data to effectively address environmental problems.
  • You'll investigate how human behavior, businesses, and governments impact the environment.
Get the brochure
Important
Although BES also has a social focus, it’s still a programme rooted in the natural sciences.

Your courses

Study programme

Your first year starts with introductory and exploratory courses, but you’ll quickly move on to building deeper knowledge and learning how to apply it to real-world sustainability challenges. You’ll also take essential subjects such as mathematics, statistics and chemistry. And of course, courses on soil processes, water and environmental technology are included in your first-year programme. By the end of the year, you’ll be able to apply your knowledge and insights in a concrete project or context.

Courses.

In the first half of your second year, you’ll take courses that prepare you for choosing your specialisation. Once you’ve made your choice, the second half of the year focuses on subjects related to your track, whether that’s the technological, social or systems-oriented side of environmental sciences.

Courses.

In your third year, you no longer take general courses. One half of the year is dedicated to completing your specialisation, and the other half is free space: you can choose a minor or create your own set of courses based on your interests.
You’ll finish your Bachelor’s with a thesis, a research project that you design yourself.

Courses.

In your third year, you choose a minor, a chance to broaden your knowledge or dive deeper into a topic you find interesting. Examples include Geo-information for Environment, Society or Natural Resource Conflict and Governance and Management of Terrestrial Ecosystem. You can also take courses at other universities in the Netherlands or abroad. Your study adviser will help you find the option that fits you best.

Check out all minors.

At WUR, we believe personal guidance and contact are very important. That's why we have significantly more support staff (lecturers, study advisers, and student counsellors) available to help you progress through your studies than at other universities in the Netherlands. This reduces the risk of you dropping out. This personal touch also enhances your learning experience, proving that we truly care about you.

The programme consists of several types of learning activities:

  • Lectures: a lecturer explains the theory to the whole class.
  • Tutorials and group work: you work on assignments with fellow students, sometimes with guidance from a teacher.
  • Practicals: you carry out experiments in a laboratory or practical room. In computer practicals, you work in a virtual environment.
  • Fieldwork and excursions: you apply theory in real situations, for example through outdoor field research.
  • Self-study: partly scheduled in your timetable, but also flexible to plan in your own time.

Some bachelor’s programs are quite similar. We've listed the key differences for you:

  • BSc Earth System Sciences
    While Environmental Sciences focuses on the entire chain of societal causes, geoscientific processes in soil, water, and the atmosphere, consequences for humans and nature, and on policy instruments and technological solutions for environmental and sustainability issues, Earth System Sciences focuses on geoscientific processes.
  • BSc Forest and Nature Management & BSc Biology
    The Bachelor’s degree in Environmental Sciences goes beyond (the management of) living nature; it also involves humans, the quality of their living environment, and the application of knowledge about organisms and ecosystems in designing solutions for environmental and sustainability issues.
  • BSc International Land and Water Management & BSc International Development Studies
    These programs focus on agricultural and development issues in developing countries. Environmental Sciences also has an international character due to the various cross-border environmental and sustainability issues it addresses.
  • BSc Biotechnology & BSc Molecular Life Sciences 
    Interconnections with these programs are mainly found in the Environmental Technology major. Environmental Sciences focuses less on the molecular level and considers the importance of social acceptance in its technical designs for sustainable solutions.
  • BSc Tourism 
    Learn how tourism contributes to economic development, the preservation of culture, nature, and the environment, and play a role in the development and implementation of sustainable tourism.

Life after this bachelor’s

After graduation

Many students pursue a master's degree after their bachelor’s degree. This allows you to gain even more knowledge and skills. These master's programs are a good fit:

  • MSc Environmental Sciences
  • MSc Urban Environmental Management
  • MSc Climate Studies
  • MSc Biobased Sciences
  • MSc Aquaculture and Marine Resource Management
  • MSc Development and Rural Innovation 

After your bachelor’s degree, you can also choose a different master's program at WUR. In your third year, with the help of your academic adviser, you'll compile courses that will prepare you well, ensuring you can progress without delay. Prefer to attend a different university or study abroad? That's often possible too, as your WUR bachelor’s degree is recognised worldwide.

This program will prepare you for employment in the Netherlands and abroad. Consider positions such as:

• Environmental researcher at the National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) or a university.
• Sustainability policy advisor at a municipality or ministry.
• Environmental and energy consultant at a consultancy firm.
• Climate adaptation project leader at NGOs or international organisations.
• Sustainability manager at companies in the food, energy, or technology sectors.

Student Career Services facilitates WUR students towards the labour market. If you need help in your orientation towards your future career. 

Good to know

Useful information

To be admitted to the bachelor’s programme Environmental Sciences, you should have studied mathematics, physics and chemistry.

Have a look at the Application & Admission page for starting at Wageningen University & Research and check whether your prior (international) education qualifies you for this bachelor’s programme. 

Are you a Dutch student? Switch the language to Dutch at the top of these pages to view the admission information that applies to you.

Studying a program costs money. Curious about the costs involved? You can find all information about the costs of this program on tution fees and study finances.

Wageningen offers a diverse, enjoyable, and amiable student community. Despite being a small town, you get to know people from all over the world because of Wageningen University & Research's global atmosphere. Everything in town is relatively accessible by bicycle, and the campus is contemporary and green. Whether it's a sporting event, a party, or a laid-back evening with friends at one of the student associations, there's always something going on. Additionally, there are parks, forests, and a river nearby, so if you enjoy the outdoors, you're in the right area.

Education of Earth Systems and Global Change

The Earth Systems and Global Change Group offers a divers educational programme in the fields of Environmental Systems Analysis (ESA) and Water Systems and Global Change (WSG). It offers education by teaching courses at the bachelor and master level of different study programs. In addition, it provides BSc and MSc theses and internships.

Thesis ESA

Thesis ESA

The Earth Systems and Global Change Group provides the possibility for students to do their thesis in the field of Environmental Systems Analysis (ESA) under supervision of a staff member of our group.

How to start a thesis at ESA?

1.   Get in touch with one of our thesis contact persons: Sverre Vink or Jana Verboom. They will inform you about further steps and give you access to all further necessary information on Brightspace.
2.   Read the ESA Thesis Course guide on Brightspace.
3.   Check Jobteaser for possible thesis topics.

Tip: Start preparing for your thesis well in advance, especially if you are planning to go abroad!

Internship ESA

Internship ESA

The Earth Systems and Global Change Group provides the possibility for students to do their internship in the field of Environmental Systems Analysis (ESA) under supervision of a staff member of our group. More information and internship opportunities in the field of Environmental Systems Analysis can be found on Brightspace. Contact the internship coordinator Sverre Vink well before the start of your internship. You cannot start your internship without approval of the internship coordinator.

Potential internship places:
  • Stage bij Sweco
  • Internship positions at IHS in Rotterdam
  • Internship in province of Zeeland

Questions about theses or internships at ESA? Contact us:

Thesis WSG

Thesis WSG

The Earth Systems and Global Change Group provides the possibility for students to do their thesis in the field of Water Systems and Global Change (WSG) under supervision of a staff member of our group.

How to start a thesis?

  1. Please register as a WSG thesis student with our secretariat by e-mailing to office.ESC@wur.nl. In your email, include your name, student number, and indicate that you would like to start a WSG thesis. You will be given access to all further necessary information on Brightspace.
  2. Read the WSG Thesis Course guide (on Brightspace) to gain all the necessary information.
  3. Check Jobteaser for possible thesis topics.
  4. Get in touch with our thesis contact person Bregje van der Bolt.
  5. Contact a potential thesis supervisor after talking to Bregje.

Tip: Start preparing for your thesis well in advance, especially if you are planning to go abroad!

Example theses

  • Climate risks analysis for sunflower farming (Todorova, 2026)
  • Machine Learning for Flood early warning (Barbieri, 2026)
  • Framing of post-flood adaptation planning (Bürgers, 2024)

Internship WSG

Internship WSG

The Earth Systems and Global Change Group provides the possibility for students to do their internship in the field of Water Systems and Global Change (WSG) under supervision of a staff member of our group.

How to start an internship?

  1. Please register as a WSG thesis student with our secretariat by e-mailing to office.ESC@wur.nl. In your email, include your name, student number, and indicate that you would like to start a WSG internship. On Brightspace you can read the WSG Internship course guide and get in touch with our internship contact person Keith Williams.
  2. WSG is occasionally alerted to internships by our partners, these are posted on Jobteaser.

Tip: Start preparing for your internship well in advance, especially if you are planning to go abroad!

Education of Environmental Technology

The Chairgroup Environmental Technology offers an education programme that is focused on sustainable technological and urban systems solutions for local and global environmental challenges. Our approach is to combine several disciplines to achieve innovations for environmental solutions.

Relevant research disciplines are a.o. biotechnology, chemical technology, microbiology, surface chemistry, organic chemistry, mass flow analysis and modelling,. We also consider the social impact of our work to be very relevant and therefore we co-operate with other University groups, such as Public Administration, Environmental Policy, Environmental Economy and Management Studies.

Thesis

Environmental Technology offers thesis tracks for various Bachelor and Master programs including the Bachelor Environmental Sciences, Master Urban Environmental Management, Master Environmental Sciences and the Master Biotechnology. Students that are interested to do a bachelor or master thesis or a research practice at our chairgroup, can choose from an extensive list of projects. To find a topic of interest please see our our dedicated Brightspace page (only available for WUR students and employees) or:

Read more in our brochure

Internship

Internship positions for students conducting their Master programme in Urban Environmental Management or Environmental Sciences can be found at the ETE Internships Brightspace site (only available for WUR students and employees). There you can discover and self-enroll at MSc Internships Environmental Technology. This is strongly advised for all students. All information about internships is provided through Brightspace.

Questions about theses or internships?

If you are interested in doing your thesis or internship at our chair group, but aren't sure about the topic yet, please contact us:

Courses offered by the Environmental Policy group

We offer a wealth of courses related to different aspects of the social and political science of environmental transformation, in both social science and interdisciplinary (environmental) programmes. For a list of courses, scroll down to the bottom of this page. We are also present in many courses offered by other chairgroups. Can’t see the forest for the trees? Be sure to ask your favourite ENP lecturer or contact the education coordinator, Mattijs Smits. 

Considering a thesis or internship at ENP? Get in touch!

You are very welcome to conduct a BSc/MSc thesis or internship at the Environmental Policy group (ENP). As a large group with experience supervising a wide range of environmental topics, we are confident we can help you succeed in your thesis or internship project. And while we are a social science group, we are very accustomed to working with students with a natural science background.

The mission of the group is to contribute to the social and political dimensions of sustainable environmental transformations. 

The broad research areas of ENP are:

  1. Circularity
  1. Biodiversity
  1. Food
  1. Climate
  1. Energy

Within and beyond these research areas there are plenty of topics to research, which we would love to explore with you!

BSc thesis

The BSc thesis often marks the end point of your BSc programme and is a great moment to practice your research skills on topics related to environmental policy and transformation. Be sure to approach lecturers during courses to discuss thesis options during your programme.

Closer to your thesis, please keep an eye out for the procedures related to your specific programme. To discuss topics, find a supervisor, or any other questions at any time, contact any of the lectures you know or our thesis coordinators Eira Carballo Cardenas and Glen Smith (see below).

MSc thesis 

The MSc thesis is a key element of your programme and an opportunity to complete an independent research project on a topic that is close to your heart. At ENP, we offer a broad range of possible topics related to the research we do on environmental transformations, from global to local and from very practical to theoretical. Check out our staff profiles and research page for inspiration. It is also possible to come up with your own topic, of course. Our team of lecturers is happy to discuss opportunities with you at any point during your MSc journey.

This journey starts when you take your courses. Feel free to approach your (guest) lecturer to discuss possible ideas for a thesis by email or in class. You can also reach out to our thesis coordinators  Eira Carballo Cardenas and Glen Smith if you need direction or inspiration.

Closer to the actual start of your thesis, we encourage you to get in touch with us (again) to be able to match you with one of our experienced supervisors. The easiest way is to write an email to any of your lecturers/coordinators, or to the thesis coordinators, no matter how (under)developed your ideas are at that point. You are also welcome to drop by our offices on the 2nd floor of the Leeuwenborch. 

BSc/MSc Internship

The internship provides the ideal format for getting work experience in the extensive field of work related to environmental transformations. We have supervised hundreds of internships at governments, companies, NGOs, banks, research institutes and other organisations, in virtually all parts of the world. 

Where to start? Your own network of classmates, friends and family can already get you on track to finding an internship opportunity. And while we don’t have off-the-shelf opportunities, feel free to approach a lecturer you know to ask about possible organisations and opportunities, whether they would be able to supervise you, and/or make an appointment with our internship coordinator.   

Internship positions are also sometimes offered by the WUR Jobseeker platform.

Found an internship position or have any other questions about the internship process? Please email internship coordinator Glen Smith with details (e.g. description of the organization, topic, type of activities, and preferred start-date). 

Support during your thesis or internship

We realise that doing a thesis or internship process can be difficult and daunting, especially when doing this for the first time. In addition to the support offered by the thesis coordinators and your supervisor, we also like students to feel part of our community. Our main vehicle for this is through the Thesis Caféthat we offer. Beyond this, you’re always welcome to attend MSc thesis presentations which are scheduled every fourth Thursday of the month (current thesis students are automatically invited, but the thesis coordinators can also let you know). Or just come by for a coffee on the second floor of the Leeuwenborch.

","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"Many disciplines in the fields of life sciences, environmental sciences and technology build on concepts from physics and chemistry. The courses General Chemistry 1 and 2 intend to make you familiar with these general concepts. Among the concepts are matter and energy, size and scale, quantization of energies, driving forces, change and equilibrium. The starting point for the exploration of the various concepts is observation of the world we live in. From there, a journey is undertaken in search of the physical and chemical laws that govern the world around us. Concepts are worked out both theoretically and experimentally in tutorials and practical classes within themes and contexts from various fields. In General Chemistry 1 the emphasis is on the concepts of size and scale, probability distributions, thermal motion, Boltzmann distribution law, driving forces behind processes, equilibrium and change, adsorption, acids and bases, and kinetics of reactions.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

This course introduces the domain and approach of the BSc Environmental Sciences programme at Wageningen University, starting from the perspective of planetary boundaries. In this course, you will be introduced to the social science and natural science foundations of this field, and learn how the synthesis of these disciplines helps to generate new interdisciplinary solutions. The course starts with introductory lectures on these topics and the nature of scientific research, followed by an in-depth case of a 'wicked' environmental problem addressing one or more planetary boundaries. The in-depth case consists of an introductory excursion and independent group work, resulting in a report and presentation in a symposium. The course also starts off several skills learning trajectories in the BES programme.

Relationships between humankind and the environment play a central role in this course. The course is subdivided into three parts: a Broad Case (BC; the topic is BSc-specific), a selected set of Information Literacy modules (IL), and the module Getting Started with Data (GSwD). For the Broad Case, students work in groups of approximately 8–9 students, with each group being supervised by a coach. In the BC, students work on complex, BSc-specific topics. For the two products students generate within the framework of the BC, they apply knowledge acquired in the Information Literacy modules. Students also receive instruction, practice, and feedback on essential skills needed to perform group work efficiently. The Getting Started with Data module is offered as a supervised, self-instructed course. It is based on a number of short instructional modules, mainly focusing on the use and analysis of data. Through this module, students become familiar with data analysis from the start of their BSc programme onwards.

Climate change, resource scarcity, and environmental degradation urge us to make a transition to a more sustainable society. This affects all sectors of the economy, but especially the nexus of energy, water, and food systems that is crucial for human subsistence. Think about CO2 emissions in energy production, increasing scarcity of drinking water, or the use of fertilizers and pesticides in agriculture. Such transitions, however, involve more than just changing production technologies; they require associated changes in infrastructure, consumer behavior, and market regulation as well. Solar panels on roofs, for example, redefine how people provide in their energy needs, the operation of the electricity grid, and energy prices. The myriad actors and factors, drivers and barriers, pathways, and policy options involved, makes them a complex challenge to study and realize.

\t\t\tTo better understand and effectuate societal transitions towards more sustainable practices, this course dives into the core concepts and frameworks of ‘sustainable development’ and ‘societal transitions’ from the perspectives of social science, policy, and history and applies them to assess the current situation, analyze past transformations, and discuss technological developments in energy, water, and food systems. As such, it provides core competences in the environmental sciences: knowledge of sustainability transitions and the capability to influence them.

\t\t\tThe course begins with a foundational week of theoretical and historical lectures on the key concepts and frameworks of ‘sustainable development’ and ‘societal transitions’ underpinning the course. It then delves deeper into sustainability transitions in the energy, water, and food systems in three thematically structured weeks. Each of these systems will be explored from the angles of Environmental History and Environmental Policy/Sociology and involve Dutch and international cases and examples. This approach allows students to gain a multidisciplinary perspective of the workings of these interrelated systems, their main challenges, and their past and future transitions.

In terms of assessment, students are required and supported to research and write an individual paper in which they are guided through stages of research and paper writing by lecturers and peer students during small group peer review sessions and one instructional tutorial. Students are required to participate in peer review activities, where they review and provide feedback on the developing papers of two other students. Finally, students are required to complete a mid-course exam.

This course introduces the occurrence, movement and quality of water over the land surface of the earth, in particular as it affects and sustains life. The course takes a geographical, mostly descriptive approach towards introducing the global hydrological cycle and water budget, hydrological processes in river catchments and groundwater, and the aquatic ecosystem. An important focus of the course is on the interdependencies between water quantity and quality in space and time.

Water Systems: Analysis was known as Water 2 until academic year 2024/2025.

This course builds upon Water Systems: Exploration (formerly known as Water 1). While the previous course emphasized 'system description,' this course shifts its focus to processes and analysis. Key topics include an introduction to physical, chemical, and biological processes in groundwater and surface waters. Students will deepen their understanding of these processes and learn to perform basic calculations related to (ground) water flow and water quality. Weekly tutorials are scheduled to practice these quantitative skills. Additionally, the course explores aspects of integrated water management.

This course focuses on soil chemical, physical and biological processes. The soil is characterized as a buffering system with water and reactive soil particles affecting mobility and bioavailability of nutrients and contaminants. This affects soil organisms, plants and groundwater and thus soil quality. Processes like water flow, leaching, adsorption, precipitation and biodegradation are introduced. Also, the role of the soil system within biogeochemical cycling of carbon and nutrients is discussed. Tutorials support the lectures with assignments. Students collect their own soil samples in the field and use these for various laboratory experiments. Practical sessions improve relevant practical skills and illustrate important topics.

introduction to environmental technology and its role in sustainable development, taking the nature and background of environmental and sustainability issues into account. Lectures deal with the various fields of application of environmental technology in water, soil and air: gaseous emissions and off-gas treatment, water pollution and wastewater treatment, soil- and groundwater contamination and remediation, and the collection, management, conversion and re-use of wastes. The most relevant state-of-the-art technology, as well as promising new technological developments will be discussed. Focus is on the biological, chemical and physical principles of the processes, as well on the design of reactors and engineered natural systems.
Working group sessions:
Design and evaluation of environmental technology requires both quantitative assessment of the fundamental of the process as well as creativity in the innovative application of technologies. Students will practice this in exercises, in which relevant processes are analysed by means of calculations and cases are discussed and solved in small groups.
Assignment coupled to lectures and excursion:
The assignment is group work (3-5 students per group) and is focused on selected environmental challenges of the world. Students choose a topic , analyse the environmental problem and define a solution while integrating the lectured knowledge into their specific topic.
The course includes an excursion to a local waste water treatment plant and a local soil remediation location to see environmental technologies in practice.
Practical training:
The practical exercises (in groups of 2-3 students) illustrate the theory of several environmental technological processes. By doing laboratory experiments on wastewater treatment and soil remediation, students get acquainted with practical aspects of environmental technology. ","type":{"code":"AK","id":"AK","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Assumed knowledge on:"}],"uid":"fdda01e3-c543-4b24-a3cb-9c4690e5a654"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

Models are often used to describe the behaviour of pollutants in environmental systems, such as the fate and transport of plastics or chemicals in surface and groundwater. These models use knowledge of physics and mathematical equations to describe the behaviour of the pollutants. In this course, the required physics is taught and applied to the context of pollution. Water quality is used as an example, and students will reflect on the relevance of similar processes for multiple spheres. Students will study and apply the physical laws relevant in environmental systems and develop basic models. In the process, they will also learn the basic skills of programming in Excel and Python. Additionally, students reflect on the modelling results, including the evaluation of performance and uncertainties. The behaviour of the pollutants will be put in the context of the relevant environmental problems.

Climate change, environmental pollution, biodiversity loss and resource depletion are interconnected crises, all caused by the way we make, use, and consume products and services. Environmental sciences integrates societal, natural and technological knowledge to understand coupled natural and socio-technical systems. They analyze how human behaviours, incentives, and institutions drive environmental change, and assess their impacts across different places and over time. Addressing these complex challenges requires understanding incentive systems, and identifying key leverage points to transform policies, practices, and technologies within global production and consumption systems.

This course focuses on analyzing sustainability challenges and exploring pathways towards circularity in contemporary global production and consumption systems. These global systems considerably affects the availability of natural resources, put pressure on marine, terrestrial and water ecosystems, while affecting societies, raising questions around equity and social justice. The approach is to analyze the sustainability challenges in one of such systems of production and consumption, starting from the end of the line (waste disposal and discharge) up to consumption, retail, transport, production and extraction of natural resources.

We investigate the entire chain, using a combination of document studies, surveys, observations, expert interviews, modelling, assessments, and reflections. This allows us to examine the environmental and societal impacts of an industry. We then explore various strategies for addressing sustainability challenges at each step of the chain. This includes analyzing innovation projects through site visits, interviews with experts and system stakeholders, and document analysis. In addition, consumer surveys will be conducted to assess preferences and willingness to pay for products made with higher environmental and social standards.

We will introduce and integrate the various knowledge domains within environmental sciences that investigate sustainability challenges, impacts, and explore possible solutions within the global production and consumption chain.

The course also enables students to develop skills in research methods, group work, intercultural communication through a collaborative research project and reflecting on their individual learning process.

Addressing the environmental and social impacts of global challenges, their underlying causes, and potential solutions requires close collaboration among diverse actors and stakeholders, as well as insights from both natural and social sciences. This course explores how various scientific disciplines and stakeholders work together to analyze and mitigate environmental problems, and how sustainable solutions can be developed. Building on first-year courses from the BES program, this course emphasizes interdisciplinary approaches to these complex problems.

The course is directed at understanding specific air quality issues in 3 themes: 1) at the local (urban), 2) regional and 3) global scale. At each scale the focus is understanding the life cycle of natural and anthropogenic air pollutants, i.e. the processes behind emission, transport in the atmosphere, chemical conversions and deposition on the land/ocean surface. The role of meteorology on air pollution mixing and transport is explicitly explained on each scale. We will pay attention at the effects on human and environmental health, as well as the feasibility of alternatives and the efficiency of regulation and policy. At the local scale the focus is on traffic and industrial emissions, the role of vegetation and photochemical smog. On the regional scale the focus is on deposition of air pollutants (clouds, precipitation, wet deposition, dry deposition), acidification and eutrophication, with ample examples by means of the nitrogen cycle. On the global scale the focus is on the tropospheric chemistry, the greenhouse effect and stratospheric ozone. Each lecture is followed by a tutorial, in which you will practice problem solving as exam training.

The air quality lectures are supported by practical activities, which are closely linked to the lecture material. In those practical activities, air quality models are confronted with observations, some of which you collect yourselves. The activities include 1) modelling local atmospheric chemistry and boundary layer dynamics with the CLASS model, 2) Modelling a Gaussian plume and comparing to measurements, 3) building NO2 samplers, collecting NO2 and PM2.5 concentration data and comparing them with the national model 4) modelling nitrogen deposition in the atmospheric boundary layer and comparing to regional observations, and 5) Moguntia: a global air quality model. The last week is the Project Week, during which you will deepen a topic of your own choice.

This course is designed to integrate and make core skills explicit within the Bachelor Environmental Sciences programme. The course builds on skills activities within courses in the first year and extends into the second year (and beyond) in which various skills are taught, practiced and assessed in different contexts. This course brings these experiences, and those obtained through extracurricular activities, together, and helps to provide students with a holistic understanding of their skills development. Personal leadership and reflection are the skills emphasized in this course to help boost the other core skills in the programme (collaboration, diversity & inclusivity, researching, social embeddedness, systems thinking, and entrepreneurial skills).

The skills addressed in this course will also help students to make better and more explicit choices in the short and longer term. In the short term, it will help students to make choices for a specialisation, thesis and (optional) internship. For the longer term, this preparation will enable them to consider their long-term goals, including further education and career opportunities.

In addition to a few lectures, most of this course consists of teacher-led and peer-led dialogues with students and alumni/professionals in environmental sciences, creating an inspiring and practical learning environment. Students will be responsible for their own progress monitoring through a portfolio.

The course is scheduled in P1_MO of the second year, but activities start in year 1 and continue in year 2.

Living in the Anthropocene means navigating a world where human activity is the dominant force shaping the planet’s climate, ecosystems, and future. However, this activity is not uniform: inequalities in wealth, power, and resource use play a central role in driving environmental degradation and shaping the distribution of its impacts. The fundamental challenge societies face lies in the tension between our current wellbeing, which often relies on exploiting and modifying environmental systems, and our collective future wellbeing, which depends on preserving, protecting, and restoring those same systems. Addressing this challenge requires confronting questions of justice—how resources are allocated between present and future generations, and how to ensure a just transition toward sustainability. Exploring these tensions is at the core of this course.

This course provides a broad and systemic overview of society’s (in)ability to address and solve environmental problems through the lens of environmental policy, economics, and law, forming a critical part of the systems thinking learning trajectory in the Environmental Sciences program. Students will explore how these disciplines interact to address complex environmental challenges, applying foundational concepts and methods in environmental economics, sociology, political science, and law to real-world cases within defined geographical and policy contexts. This approach introduces students with concepts and skills needed to analyze and tackle complex, often transboundary environmental problems characterized by uncertainties, knowledge gaps, diverging social interests, and conflicting views.

The course builds on integration of the disciplinary knowledge on Earth system processes such a hydrology, meteorology and biogeochemistry. It introduces the systems approach to study Earth system dynamics involving different temporal and spatial scales in process interactions and feedback mechanisms that explain observed climate- and global change. Emphasis is on Earth system interactions associated with dynamical, physical and biogeochemical processes affecting the state of the atmosphere, biosphere and hydrosphere under natural and anthropogenic conditions. ","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"The course introduces Geo-Information Science and its scientific and societal interests. The starting point of the introduction is the geo-information cycle. This cycle frames geo data based actions like acquisition and storage, processing and visualization. It is explained that these actions can be used to describe, to analyse, to design and to realize real world phenomena. Thus geo data is always acquired, processed and visualized with a specific purpose. This is illustrated via the conceptual, formal and technical modelling steps.
Important in these modelling steps are the roles of geographical data attributes (thematic, geometric, temporal). Because the acquisition and processing of geo data is purposive, meta data plays an important role to find geo data and geo data processing steps. It also is important to evaluate the (re)usability of geo data and geo data processing steps. Meta data explain important geo data characteristics like (geo)reference, map projection and available attributes. Geo-visualization, especially cartography concepts, is introduced to show how geo data ought to be communicated. After the introduction of the geo data related concepts, the course offers the geo data processing options. The latter is done by the introduction of three data handling classes (query, transform and alter) and the data-action model. The geo data that represent terrain height and processing of these elevation data has given notice. Besides, basic concepts of Remote Sensing (spectral signature, sensor types, visual and quantitative processing) are also introduced. The application of all concepts is practiced during a practical and by a small project using professional software and data according a working procedure.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

  • present small project results by a technical report that describes the application procedure and by a slide presentation that shows the application results.

Microbiology and Toxicology is a basic course, which is compulsory for BFT (first year of study) and BES (second year of study). The course is composed of Microbiology and Toxicology lectures, and a Microbiology practical.
The Toxicology part deals with the basic concepts of Toxicology: the study of adverse effects that chemical substance may have on living organisms. The field of Toxicology integrates aspects of e.g. biology, pharmacology and biochemistry. The lectures will focus on which chemicals are toxic, what potential effects chemicals may have and a general introduction into the assessment of risks that chemicals may pose to humans and the environment. All will be illustrated with relevant cases on environmental risks of chemicals and risks related to food.
The Microbiology part deals with basic features of microbial cells (prokaryotes and microbial eukaryotes), history of microbiology, diversity of microbes, structure and function of cells, microbial metabolism, energy yielding reactions, fermentation and respiration, photosynthesis, growth, and nutrient cycles. The importance of microbes for life on earth is explained. At the end of the course it should be clear that microbes play an essential role in every-day life, even more than you ever anticipated. Moreover, microbes are important for various types of applied research, in the areas of food, health and environment. Microbes are important for improving the “quality of life”.

In this course, students will integrate their knowledge of two-year Bachelor Environmental Sciences (or equivalent) in a field-based transdisciplinary research project on (an) environmental challenge(s). The course is set up to provide a comprehensive, interdisciplinary, and hands-on learning experience. It focuses on addressing complex environmental challenges through case studies conducted in collaboration with external commissioners from e.g. industry or public institutions. These applied projects require students to work in intercultural settings, engaging with local communities, experts, and stakeholders, fostering an understanding of diverse cultural, social, and ecological perspectives. The field work will take place in an international context involving local stakeholders and (a) real life case(s). Students will be involved in preparing for, doing, and reporting and reflecting on field work abroad during this course. By adopting a trans- and interdisciplinary approach, students integrate knowledge from various fields, blending scientific, policy, and societal insights to co-create innovative solutions to pressing environmental issues.

Furthermore, the course emphasizes self-reflection as a core component, encouraging students to critically evaluate their personal growth, teamwork dynamics, and cultural and societal boundary crossing ability. This reflective process deepens their understanding of their role in collaborative projects and prepares them to tackle future environmental challenges with adaptability and cultural sensitivity.

Humanity faces the interconnected crises of increasing pollution, accelerating climate change, and unprecedented biodiversity loss. These challenges are deeply interwoven: pollution from industrial, agricultural, and urban sources contributes to climate forcing and degrades ecosystems; climate change disrupts ecological processes, amplifies pollution impacts, challenges agricultural production, and threatens species and habitats; biodiversity loss, in turn, reduces ecosystem and agricultural resilience and undermines natural capacities to regulate climate and buffer pollution. Actions aimed at mitigating one challenge can inadvertently worsen another, while well-designed interventions can create powerful synergies across the nexus.

This course supports students in developing the capacity to understand and analyze complex interactions between pollution, climate and biodiversity using systems thinking and systems analysis approaches. The course combines conceptual and empirical approaches to achieve this understanding. Through activities such as identifying feedback loops, mapping cross-scale interactions, and exploring potential leverage points, students learn to interpret how pollution, climate processes, and biodiversity dynamics drive coupled human–environment systems. By mapping stakeholders related to the nexus, and by integrating stakeholders’ and academic knowledge and perspectives, students will understand the complexity of navigating trade-offs and finding solutions. Students will also examine how governance, technology, and other societal choices shape the emergence of trade-offs and synergies across the nexus. Students will integrate selected aspects of the systems knowledge they acquired into a prototype representation of the system, e.g. a serious game prototype.

By combining analytical and reflective skills, this course prepares students to engage with sustainability challenges that transcend disciplinary and sectoral boundaries. Students gain the ability to contribute to discussions and decisions on resilient, equitable, and transformative pathways that harmonize pollution control, climate stabilization, and biodiversity protection within planetary boundaries.

This course uses examples from agricultural and food systems throughout. Agricultural and food systems, through their land use (change) and diverse management practices, are major drivers of environmental and social outcomes. Understanding the role of agriculture and assessing the negative and positive impacts of different agricultural approaches is therefore of key importance for navigating the pollution-climate-biodiversity nexus.

In short, the course aims to enable students to understand, analyze, and evaluate the interconnections between pollution, climate, and biodiversity using systems thinking and analysis tools, and to apply this knowledge to identify and assess solutions that foster sustainable and resilient social-ecological systems.

This course offers an overview of how international and EU law responds to today’s most pressing environmental problems. It shows which unique solutions, and problems, the legal system presents in addressing these environmental problems. We discuss topics such as climate change, biodiversity, and the role of human rights. Overarching themes include the interaction and overlap of national, regional and international legal systems in addressing environmental problems, and the role of individuals in these processes. In order to provide students with a solid foundation, fundamentals of national, EU and international (environmental) law are also set out, leading to the development of legal skills and knowledge that students can use beyond the current course.

The course provides an introduction to environmental economics and is developed for students of non-economic study programmes. It is also suitable as an introduction to environmental economics for students of economic study programmes. The aim of the course is to show how environmental problems can be approached and analysed using economic theory. Furthermore, the course demonstrates how economics provides guidance to address serious environmental problems such as climate change, ozone depletion, air and water pollution at different scales (global, regional). In particular, the course will establish the foundations of environmental economics. The students will learn how markets function and under which conditions markets fail, giving rise to a misallocation of resources causing environmental problems. These insights will then be used to analyse how policy interventions can correct market failure and enhance social welfare. The course also introduces students to recent policy developments regarding environmental and sustainability issues.

The course consists of classroom lectures and tutorials. The economic concepts introduced in the lectures are applied to a number of case studies of important environmental issues and environmental problems such as, for example, pollution control. To deepen the understanding of economic concepts, students will have to work on assignments during tutorials. The aim of the assignments is to practice with the theories and methods acquired during the lectures. Students also learn how to analyze economic data, run simple regression models to draw evidence-based conclusions about environmental outcomes. In addition, students write a scientific essay (individual paper) about an environmental economics and policy topic. The aim is to learn how to apply the acquired theoretical knowledge to selected environmental economics and policy issues, how to compile and structure information and to learn scientific working skills. Students are expected to attend all lectures and tutorials and to prepare themselves by studying the reading material prior to the lectures.

Access to energy is a key prerequisite for any industrial society. Fossil fuels are the dominant energy source nowadays, but their use involves a number of problems: enhanced greenhouse effect, air pollution, and resource depletion. Energy savings and the use of renewable energy are directions for achieving an environmentally sustainable industrial society. This course will focus on the use and conversion of renewable energy sources as a key factor in solving environmental problems. Thermodynamics will be taught and used to analyze the necessary energy conversion processes.

  • General safety while working in the lab
  • Hazardous substances/ chemicals

At WUR we value your safety. Going into the field for an excursion or for observations/ measurements exposes you to specific risks some of which you'd take for granted while visiting nature or urban environments outside the university perspective. Things like traffic or uneven terrain seems something that you face on a day to day basis, but need a more strict approach while facing them in a professional way. Furthermore infection prevention and social responsible behavior are topics that require specific attention. Therefore many measures are taken in order to facilitate a safe study in Wageningen.
And although all these measures are in place still one of the most important factors for a safe stay is YOUR behavior and knowledge of these measures. Therefore the Fieldwork Safety course is mandatory for all students going into the field for their education.
This course will introduce you to safe fieldwork during courses at WUR and will cover a range of topics:

  • how to prepare for fieldwork;
  • what risk can you be exposed to when working in the field.
